11197-bambi:
Marjorie Benton Cooke's 1914 novel follows Francesca Parkhurst, called Bambi, the quick-witted daughter of a professor who raised her to be happy without teaching her how to earn a living. When she marries Jarvis, a serious playwright, she sets out to support them both by writing popular stories, clashing with his highbrow ideals and her own ambitions. New York theater life supplies the backdrop.

The novel's charm lies in Bambi's talk: fast, funny, and determined to bend the world to her plans. Beneath the comedy runs a question about marriage and work, as husband and wife negotiate whose art pays the bills. Cooke's best-known book, it captures a moment when women writers were claiming commercial success openly.
16351-critical-and-historical-essays-lec:
Edward MacDowell's Critical and Historical Essays, edited by W. J. Baltzell and published in 1912, shows the composer as a writer on music. In 1896 Columbia University offered MacDowell its newly created chair of music, and he accepted after much thought, becoming one of America's leading composers in a new academic role. His lectures turn from composition to history and aesthetics.

Chapters trace the origin of music and song, the music of Hebrews, Hindus, Egyptians, Assyrians, and Chinese, then Greece, Rome, and the early church. Scale, notation, Hucbald and Guido, counterpoint, instruments, and folk song follow. Music students will find a clear, humane survey from a composer who loved the past.
23213-uncle-wiggily-and-old-mother-hubba:
Howard R. Garis published Uncle Wiggily and Old Mother Hubbard in 1922, a children's book in his long Uncle Wiggily series. The rabbit gentleman at its centre steps into the world of Mother Goose. Its chapter list reads like a roll call of nursery-rhyme figures.

Uncle Wiggily meets Mother Goose herself, then the three little pigs, one by one. He also meets Little Boy Blue, Little Bo-Peep, and Tommie Tucker, among others. Each short chapter gives young readers a fresh small adventure, built from rhymes they may already know by heart.
27975-delineations-of-the-ox-tribe-the-n:
George Vasey published Delineations of the Ox Tribe in London in 1851, with seventy-two wood engravings by the author, dedicated to William Yarrell. The book gives the natural history of bulls, bisons, and buffaloes, exhibiting all known species and remarkable varieties of the genus Bos.

Vasey admits that known facts do not yet allow dividing the genus into sub-genera, and he brings together descriptions of individual specimens with new facts of his own. The frontispiece shows the Sanga or Galla ox of Abyssinia, and the volume is a handsome example of mid-Victorian zoology.
33091-a-volunteer-with-pike-the-true-nar:
Robert Ames Bennet's Volunteer with Pike tells the true narrative of Dr. John Robinson and his love for the fair Señorita Vallois. It was published in Chicago in 1909 with four color illustrations by Charlotte Weber-Ditzler. Its chapters run from the rose in the mire and plain Thomas Jefferson through the president's house and Señorita Alisanda. They go on to gulf and barrier, the web of the plotter, ship and crew, and the hospitable Blennerhassetts. They then turn to the father of waters, General Wilkinson, and the Pawnee peril.

Bennet, author of For the White Christ and Into the Primitive, sets his volunteer beside Zebulon Pike's expedition to the Grand Peak. The author dedicates the journey to his father, who followed after Pike half a century later. It remains a lively historical adventure, grounded in a real expedition and told with the color of its period.
33434-the-squirrels-and-other-animals-or:
George Waring's Squirrels and Other Animals, published in London, illustrates the habits and instincts of many smaller British quadrupeds. It opens with a squirrel waking as spring warmth stirs it from sleep. Its chapters follow foxes, hedgehogs, and other small beasts through their daily lives. Waring writes for young naturalists.

The book's charm lies in its gentle, story-like natural history, where animals speak and act in ways children can follow. Its pictures, including the fox and the hedgehog, add to the delight. For readers who love British wildlife, it is a pleasing, old-fashioned guide to the small creatures of field and wood.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-al: Albi's council of 1254, held by St Louis on his return from an unlucky crusade, aimed at stamping out what remained of the Albigensian heresy and reforming clergy and people. Zoen, Bishop of Avignon and papal legate, presided, and its decrees also legislated concerning the Jews. St Louis called the synod while homeward bound, turning from crusade to the ordering of his realm's church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hammurabi:
Hammurabi, sixth king of the first Babylonian dynasty, is known both as a conqueror and as a lawgiver whose code made him famous. His reign's dates are disputed, from about 2130 to about 1950 before Christ. In his thirtieth year he broke Elam's yoke, took Larsa, and called himself King of Sumer and Akkad, knitting north and south Babylonia into one empire.

Letters and chronicles show a ruler busy every year with temples, canals, farming, and justice, in a reign of great literary activity. Scholars link him plausibly with Amraphel of Genesis 14. His Code, cut on a black diorite stele found at Susa in 1901 and now in the Louvre, set his name among antiquity's greatest rulers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-de-albi: Juan de Albi, also called Alba, was a Spanish Carthusian of Val-Christ near Segovia who died on 27 December 1591. Skilled in Eastern languages, above all Hebrew, he was known as a learned commentator on Scripture. His single recorded work, a commentary of notes and selections from both Testaments, appeared at Valencia in 1610 and was reissued at Venice in 1613.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lesbi:
Lesbi was a titular see in Mauretania Sitifensis, suffragan of Sitifis, or Setif, in Algeria. It is not the island of Lesbos, as some state; Lesbos never was a titular bishopric and holds two titular archbishoprics instead, Mytilene and Methymna. All we know of Lesbi comes from the Itinerarium Antonini: it lay twenty-five miles distant from Tupusuctu, or Tiklat, and eighteen miles off Horrea Aninici, now Ain-Roua, south of Bougie.

The town therefore stood on the Sava, that is, the Oued-Bou-Sellam, but no remains are to be seen. Only two of its bishops are recorded: Romanus, a Donatist at the Carthage conference of 411, and Vadius, a Catholic exiled by King Huneric in 484.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-urbi-et-orbi:
Urbi et Orbi, meaning for the city and for the world, marks a papal document addressed not only to Rome but to the whole Catholic world. The phrase belongs especially to the solemn blessing with plenary indulgence which, before Rome's occupation, the pope gave on set occasions from the balcony of the city's chief basilicas. It was imparted yearly at St Peter's on Holy Thursday, Easter, and the feast of Sts Peter and Paul.

It was also given at St John Lateran on the Ascension and at St Mary Major on the Assumption. Extraordinary occasions brought it too, such as a coronation, an enthronement, or a holy year for pilgrims. The entry explains the blessing's form, its indulgences, and its history, including the Ascension blessing. It gives readers a compact guide to one of the papacy's most public rites.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIDallasFieldO:
Harold Weisberg wrote to Julia Shea on June 11, 1980 about a records fight with the FBI's Dallas field office. Weisberg had filed Privacy Act requests for files the office held. He reports that the office complied only in part and withheld records he believed were his to see.

The letter is a progress report from a long campaign of requests and appeals. Weisberg spent years forcing assassination records out of the Bureau, office by office. Dallas held central files on the Kennedy case, so its refusals mattered. His account to Shea preserves the state of that fight in mid-1980.
nasa-tm-19700032560-erosion-of-a-three-s:
G. M. Kaplan of the Lewis Research Center and E. Schnetzer of the General Electric Company wrote this paper for a 1970 energy conference in Las Vegas. It reports blade erosion in a three-stage potassium vapor turbine. NASA had worked on such turbines since 1961.

An earlier two-stage turbine had run for thousands of hours in tests. A three-stage machine then finished its own long endurance run. Wet potassium vapor can chew at turbine blades over time. The paper reports the erosion found after the long test. Such turbines were candidates for making electricity in space from a nuclear heat source.
podcast-joerogan-P7xu0t9dTbI:
Filmmaker Bart Sibrel joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2141 to make his case that the moon landings were faked. Sibrel has spent decades on the claim, confronting astronauts and building films around the footage he calls staged. Rogan gives the skeptic a full hearing.

Sibrel lays out his best points, from flag movement to radiation belts, and tells of his run-ins with the Apollo crew. Rogan tests the arguments and asks what proof would change Sibrel's mind. The episode preserves the moon-hoax case in its most committed form, useful for anyone who wants to hear it whole before judging it.
podcast-tuckercarlson-orgvAk7JhBI:
Professor Dave Collum joins Tucker Carlson for a year-end style talk that roams very wide. The title names a financial crisis, Diddy, energy weapons, QAnon, and the deep state's shift to digital tools. Collum teaches chemistry and talks markets on the side.

Collum gives his blunt read on debt, banks, and the risk of a crash. He then roams into crime tales, secret tech, and the tales that swirl online. Carlson lets him range and jumps in with his own takes. Listeners get a free-wheeling talk with a sharp, funny guest. The library holds it as a record of the chat.
